{{Short description|Decomposition of real-valued functions}}
[[File:Positive and Negative Parts of f(x) = x^2 - 4.png|thumb|Positive and Negative Parts of {{math|1=''f''(''x'') = ''x''<sup>2</sup> − 4}}]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''positive part''' of a [[real number|real]] or [[extended real number line|extended real]]-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]] is defined by the formula
<math display="block"> f^+(x) = \max(f(x),0) = \begin{cases}
f(x) & \text{ if } f(x) > 0 \\
0 & \text{ otherwise.}
\end{cases} </math>

Intuitively, the [[graph of a function|graph]] of <math>f^+</math> is obtained by taking the graph of <math>f</math>, 'chopping off' the part under the {{math|''x''}}-axis, and letting <math>f^+</math> take the value zero there.

Similarly, the '''negative part''' of {{math|''f''}} is defined as 
<math display="block"> f^-(x) = \max(-f(x),0) = -\min(f(x),0) = \begin{cases}
-f(x) & \text{ if } f(x) < 0 \\
0 & \text{ otherwise}
\end{cases} </math>

Note that both {{math|''f''<sup>+</sup>}} and {{math|''f''<sup>&minus;</sup>}} are non-negative functions. A peculiarity of terminology is that the 'negative part' is not negative (like the imaginary part of a [[complex number]] is not imaginary).

The function {{math|''f''}} can be expressed in terms of {{math|''f''<sup>+</sup>}} and {{math|''f''<sup>&minus;</sup>}} as
<math display="block"> f = f^+ - f^-. </math>

Also note that
<math display="block"> |f| = f^+ + f^-.</math>

Using these two equations one may express the positive and negative parts as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
f^+ &= \frac{|f| + f}{2} \\
f^- &= \frac{|f| - f}{2}.
\end{align}</math>

Another representation, using the [[Iverson bracket]] is
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 f^+ &=  [f>0]f \\
 f^- &= -[f<0]f.
\end{align}</math>

One may define the positive and negative part of any function with values in a [[linearly ordered group]].

The unit [[ramp function]] is the positive part of the [[identity function]].

==Measure-theoretic properties==
Given a [[sigma-algebra|measurable space]] {{math|(''X'', Σ)}}, an extended real-valued function {{math|''f''}} is [[measurable function|measurable]] [[if and only if]] its positive and negative parts are. Therefore, if such a function {{math|''f''}} is measurable, so is its absolute value {{math|{{abs|''f''}}}}, being the sum of two measurable functions. The converse, though, does not necessarily hold: for example, taking {{math|''f''}} as
<math display="block">f = 1_V - \frac{1}{2},</math>
where {{math|''V''}} is a [[Vitali set]], it is clear that {{math|''f''}} is not measurable, but its absolute value is, being a constant function.

The positive part and negative part of a function are used to define the [[Lebesgue integral]] for a real-valued function. Analogously to this decomposition of a function, one may decompose a [[signed measure]] into positive and negative parts &mdash; see the [[Hahn decomposition theorem]].
